text: Three words explain why Europe crossed an ocean: God, gold, and glory. Not curiosity. Not science. Three hungers — and they were strong enough to sail into the blank part of the map. You're watching APUSH Explained. Let's get into it.

Last video, we saw the three worlds on the eve of contact. Now the question: why did Europe move first? [pause:0.45] Here's the setup. By the 1400s, tiny Portugal has invented the ship that can do it — the caravel, with lateen sails and a hull that can beat back upwind across the Atlantic. Spain, fresh from driving the Moors out of Granada in 1492, has crusading energy and a queen willing to gamble.

And both are starving for the same thing: a sea route to Asia's spices that doesn't run through Muslim middlemen. The point is: nobody sailed west for adventure. They sailed for profit, prayer, and pride.

First, the three motives — and yes, you need all three, because the exam loves asking which one mattered most. Gold: the literal kind. Europe is cash-hungry, and the legend says Asia is paved with it. God: convert the heathen, outflank Islam, carry the cross around the globe. Glory: kings compete like athletes — whoever plants the flag first wins. [pause:0.75] Three motives, one ocean. Now watch how each one played out.
Gold first. Columbus writes home from Jamaica in 1503, shipwrecked and desperate — and listen to what obsession sounds like:

quote.source: Christopher Columbus, letter from Jamaica to Ferdinand and Isabella

text: “Gold is most excellent; gold is treasure, and he who possesses it does all he wishes to in this world.”

He's not describing wealth. He's describing a religion. [pause:0.45] And here's the kicker — he found almost no gold. The obsession outran the evidence by decades. But the obsession was enough to keep the ships coming.
Now God. Richard Hakluyt, England's great promoter of colonization, sells the queen on planting colonies in 1584. His pitch, in his own spelling:

quote.source: Richard Hakluyt, Discourse of Western Planting

text: “Wee shall by plantinge there inlarge the glory of the Gospell.”

Planting — that's his word for colonizing. Gardens, not conquests. [pause:0.45] Historians still argue how much was faith and how much was cover for greed. The honest answer: the same man could pray on Sunday and count gold on Monday. The tension is the point.

Second: the sequence. Because motives don't move ships — voyages do. [pause:0.45] 1492: Granada falls in January; Columbus sails in August and lands in October. 1493: he returns with seventeen ships — colonization starts immediately. 1498: the third voyage reaches the South American mainland. 1502: the fourth voyage, wrecked off Jamaica. [pause:0.75] And 1507: a German mapmaker reads the voyage accounts and names the new continent after Amerigo Vespucci — America.

Look at the route. [pause:0.45] Out from Spain, southwest on the trade winds — that's the easy part; the wind does the work. Landfall in the Bahamas. Then the brutal part: beating back northeast against those same winds, which is why the return took twice as long. [pause:0.75] Four voyages, eleven years, and Columbus never once sets foot on the North American mainland. He dies in 1506 still insisting he'd found Asia. The point is: the man who started it all never understood what he'd started.

Third: glory — and who else wanted it. Spain's rivals watched and copied, each in their own style. France sent Cartier up the St. Lawrence chasing furs, not gold — trading posts, not plantations. England tried Roanoke in 1587 — the Lost Colony, vanished without a trace. [pause:0.45] And England invented the financial weapon that would beat them all: the joint-stock company. Investors pool money, share the risk, share the profit. [TIP]Remember this: joint-stock companies are how England colonized on the cheap — private money, public empire.[/TIP]

So the point is this. God, gold, and glory didn't just launch ships — they designed three different empires. Spain's hunger for gold built a conquest machine. France's fur trade built alliances. England's investors built settler colonies. [pause:0.75] Same ocean, three motives, three Americas. And here's the callback to our first video: every one of those empires was built on the catastrophe we saw in the Florentine Codex — the emptying of Native America made room for all of it.

That's why Europe sailed west — God, gold, and glory, in that order of honesty. Next: the machine Spain built on the wreckage — forced labor, silver mountains, and a racial hierarchy painted in sixteen panels. That's vid-u1-04, plus the drill set. Drill it, own it — I'll see you in the next one.
